en: Let me test myself against you.
I will pull the reins
And turn the ever-ready Taibuurul,
Then drive you toward Beijing.
After making me pay beyond all measure,
After splitting my head open,
How can I remain alive!”
The splendid lion, proud as a rooster,
The noble hero who would not be moved—
After his father Manas died,
He settled and took possession of Talas;
Living as an orphan, he grew to manhood
And became hero Semetey.
He had not yet died of shame,
And had never before seen
Such humiliation upon the earth.
Without looking around him,
Without sparing his life at all,
Without glancing about,
Your champion, son of the mighty man,
Did not value his life as much as a hair.
He hurriedly put on bulletproof Akolpok
Without even shaking it out,
And mounted the playful Buurul
Bare-backed at a bound.
He seized and swung
The white whip with a black handle,
And struck Buurul’s flank,
Making it ring out, “Kang!”
With no spear and only a whip,
The leopard’s offspring
Set out to chase Karagul almost naked.
He looked neither uphill nor down,
Gave no thought to dying,
And raced in fury.
As though the horse could understand speech,
He pleaded with Buurul:
“My beloved Arbuudan,
Lower your head toward the ground
And take a different kind of stride.
To the one who has never squatted down to urinate,
Whose sleeve has never touched the ground.
That infidel son of Katal—
Bring me up to him once.
Lower your neck toward the earth,
My beloved noble thoroughbred,
And take a stride beyond all measure.
That infidel son of Kaldai,
Hero Khan Kongurbai—
His Black Horse ridden on patrol,
Bring me up to it once!
I raise argamaks and horses;
May I circle in devotion, Buurul,
Around a thoroughbred like you!
I gathered champions and heroes;
May I circle around a kinsman like you!
When he made me pay beyond all measure,
When he split my head open,
If only he had turned his neck before me,
If only Külchoro had stood and watched—
Would that thundering Karagul
Then have dared commit this deed?
The dream he saw had turned baleful—
“Have you heard of the deed
Of the man who came on patrol and split my head?”
Turning wrathful and transformed,
Ready to tear Karagul apart if he caught him,
He spoke threats against him.
Breaking the ground beneath his tread,
The noble lord mounted Buurul bare-backed
And raced away.
Such was the nature of Buurul:
His destiny was to be ridden into battle;
That bastard horse Buurul
Was Semetey’s wing.
It was his custom to chase down
An enemy who fled before him.
There was no hillock as large as an ankle-bone,
No hollow as broad as a saddlecloth,
No furrow touched by a plow,
No burrow dug by a marmot;
Whenever he came upon such terrain,
It was his custom to run all the harder.
If the desert was forty days across,
If the country was harsh and difficult,
It was his custom to endure.
When he saw the hero’s bearing
And reached the rolling ridges,
Buurul lengthened his stride;
His legs drove down like an argali’s.
When he began to climb uphill,
His mane and tail spread wide.
Kongurbai’s Algara
Thundered his hooves upon the ground;
In Semetey’s horse Buurul’s throat,
The black-steel bit
Clattered against his palate.
When they entered the downslope,
Kongurbai’s Algara
Ran far ahead, shimmering like a mirage.
When they began to climb uphill,
Semetey’s Buurul
Closed upon his heels and hemmed him in.
Buurul ran in haste;
When Karagul, son of Katal,
Saw how he ran,
“What has happened to that dog?” he said.
Despairing of his splendid life,
He crossed rough, hummocked ground,
Passed over rugged, rolling ridges,
And the mighty man fled before him.
Such was the precious sight:
The two went like bride and groom.
They traveled on through haze
Over rugged ridges;
The coursers dug up
The black earth as they went.
Algara and Karagul
Hurried onward.
They traveled through a hazy land
Beyond the reach of sight.
They traveled through the desert,
Ending in a dim and hazy point.
They went along the far side
Of rugged ridges
And level uplands beyond sight.
Such was the nature of the courser;
Karagul, who had deceived the hero,
Put his trust in his racer
And fled in boundless haste.
Where Algara’s and Taibuurul’s
Hooves struck squarely,
The ground was cut like a great canal;
Their precisely planted tracks
Were carved like the hull of a ship.
Such was the nature of the coursers:
Their mouths gaped like saws,
And blood-mingled white foam
From the bereft, ill-fated horse
Scattered across his breast.
Toward Dyngsha on this side of Beijing,
He went onward, leaning low;
His forelock tangled and matted,
His splendid head, broad as a basin,
Was covered in red dust.
They lowered their heads toward the earth
And ran in an extraordinary way;
They stretched their necks toward the ground
And took strides beyond measure.
Algara and noble Buurul—
No wind could match their gallop,
No beast could match their tread.
When they reached certain places,
A ground-hugging fog rose like a mirage.
Such was the nature of the racer:
The Bloodthirsty One’s Buurul
Drew near to Algara.
Look well upon the plight of Karagul,
This doomed man here!
His speech was clear when he spoke;
Keen-eyed, he was a judge of horses.
When he saw the speed
Of Buurul beneath Semetey,
He feared a messenger
Of Kakanchin’s Beijing might hear,
Or, if not that dog, a scout
Might come out before him.
He feared they would begin a fierce spear-fight
And separate him
From the champion son of the Bloodthirsty One.
Shouting in fury,
Raising the battle cry, “Kakan!”
He crossed and went beyond
A pass shaped like a saddle-back.
“If my wretched life falls into his hands,
What dreadful thing will happen?”
Thinking this, Karagul
Fled onward in haste—
Karagul, chief of the horse herders,
This one doomed to vanish.
When he saw Buurul’s bearing,
Fearing the raging Burut would catch him,
Fearing he would cut off his head,
He fled onward.
“Will I catch him?” Buurul wondered,
And raced in haste.
Lengthening his stride like an argali,
His eyes reddening like a lion’s,
The land streamed by like a mirage;
The creature ran like a gazelle,
Drew near to Karagul,
And came close upon his heels.
At that time Karagul—
Such was the plight of Karagul—
Longed desperately to reach
The city of the Kakanchin.
Out on the plain on this side,
His heart became deeply troubled;
Karagul floundered along,
Looking as though he would die.
Algara ran sluggishly,
And Karagul suffered bitterly.
His eyes darted wildly,
And his legs began to dangle.
He struck Algara beneath him
From side to side with his whip,
Spurring him on both flanks.
“What has happened to this dog?” he thought;
Afraid for his life and frantic,
Karagul hurried desperately
And spoke to Algara:
“Algara of the accursed khan,
You were the khan’s own horse.
Your condition is not that of a worn-out old beast;
My fly-sized life is under strain,
And this is no time for you to cease running.
Algara, whom I mounted in trust,
You have brought moonless night
Down upon Karagul’s head—
You have brought the day of death upon me.
At the champion son of the Bloodthirsty One,
At the misbegotten foe who fixed his malice on me,
It seems I will suffer humiliation while alive.
If by chance I fall into his hands,
Before my allotted day has ended,
It seems I will die upon the open plain.
Could such misery, such a ruinous affair—
Algara running like a wild beast—
Ever have existed even in a dream?
I wear a bright red and green coat;
Its trim will not tear when I pull it.
I was deceived by a strange road;
If I fall into his hands, that Burut
Does not look like one who will turn aside.
It seems he may catch me;
That calamity-bringing Burut
Will drag me along the road
And make me fit for the Danggits, it seems.”
Thus Karagul
Grieved in this way.
How could Semetey hold back?
He pursued Karagul bare-backed.
A hero born surpassing
His father Manas, the gray wolf,
He bore down upon
The great plain, broad as the moon.
If you ask of that plain,
Haze descends and makes corners upon it,
And it ends in a dim and shadowed point.
When one looks, nothing catches the eye;
In this accursed world,
One cannot tell where anything lies.
The sight arrests the heart;
Jutting up in stark ridges,
The mountain’s summit cannot be seen.
